1


ARGUMENT IN REPLY
Respondent’s argument largely rests on two
premises: either that federal statutes never adopt
state substantive rules (except, perhaps, for “housekeeping” rules), or, alternatively, that something special about the federal eminent domain power requires
ignoring state substantive just -compensation rules
when private parties take land. Each one is false.
To begin, this Court has consistently looked to
state law to lend substance to federal statutes—originally because it believed this was mandatory, and
later because it believed this was wise, but consistently nonetheless. The default rule in 1947, like the
default rule today, was that state law would govern
unless Congress did something to set it aside.
And nothing about either eminent domain in
general or the Natural Gas Act in particular is different. Respondent insists that “the right of eminent domain” was, in 1947, a term of art  that incorporated
federal just -compensation rules , but this Court’s
cases directly say otherwise. To be sure, the United
States itself is not required to follow state substantive
rules when it takes land in its own name, but that is
because the United States is sovereign —it is always
immune from state laws. All of Respondent’s eminentdomain cases simply reflect the basic rule that the
United States can ignore state law when condemning
land just as it can any other time . Respondent has
found no case suggesting that private condemnors can
do the same, and nothing in the statute purports to
implement the federal constitutional floor as a uniform nationwide ceiling on compensation.

2


With those false premises set aside, Respondent has little to offer, asking this Court to rely on unrelated language in unrelated statutes as a guide to
interpreting the statute here, to overread this Court’s
only decision interpreting this subsection of the statute, or to jettison the question presented altogether.
These arguments are wrong as well, and the decision
below should be reversed.
A. Unless displaced by Congress , s tate
substantive law ordinarily provides
the default rule.
As explained in the opening brief,  at the time
Congress adopted 15 U.S.C. § 717f(h), the prevailing
rule was (and long had been) that state substantive
law controlled in federal litigation unless it was expressly or implicitly preempted. Opening Br. 26  (citing Agency Holding Corp.  v. Malley-Duff & Assocs.,
Inc., 483 U.S. 143, 158  (1987) (Scalia, J., concurring
in the judgment) ). In other words, the rule was that
state law controlled “in the absence of explicit legislative policy cutting across state interests.” Bd. of
Comm’rs of Jackson C nty. v. United States, 308 U.S.
343, 351–52 (1939); see also Br. for Resp. 17–18 & n.5
(citing Jackson Cnty.). That tradition was ratified by
the Rules of Decision Act. 28 U.S.C. §  1652. And it
lives on today in this Court’s decision in United States
v. Kimbell Foods , Inc. , 440 U.S. 715 (1979) , which
says that courts should look to state law in the absence of an express or implicit requirement to do otherwise. Opening Br. 37. To be sure, state law does not
always control because it is often trumped by the Supremacy Clause, which overrides laws that “regulate
the Government directly or discriminate against

3


it . . . [or] conflict with an affirmative command of
Congress.” North Dakota v. United States, 495 U.S.
423, 434 (1990) (plurality). But without one of those,
longstanding tradition points to state law.
Respondent does not deny the existence of this
tradition. Instead, it claims (at 41) that the tradition
was limited to “housekeeping rules” like statutes of
limitations.1 But that simply isn’t true —to the contrary, by the middle of the 1940s, this Court had already recognized that its “custom of resorting to [state
laws] to give meaning and content to federal statutes
[was] too old and its use too diversified” to allow concerns for national uniformity to trump state law
across the board. Davies Warehouse Co. v. Bowles, 321
U.S. 144, 155 (1944). Perhaps Respondent would say
that the law at issue in Bowles (the meaning of the
term “public utility,” which this Court held was controlled by state law, id. at 154) was also a “housekeeping” law, but it’s hard to see why. Indeed, the opinion
says otherwise, justifying its rule by reference to traditional state authority over “acquisition, transmission, and transfer of property[.]” Id. at 155.2

1 This Court has not historically divided substantive
rules into “housekeeping” and non- “housekeeping” categories.
Indeed, to the extent that this Court has a jurisprudence of
“housekeeping rules,” its  cases suggest that statutes of limitations fall outside that category. See Chevron Oil Co. v. Huson,
404 U.S. 97, 103–04 & n.6 (1971) (applying state statute of limitations in part because “state time limitation[s]” were not “mere
‘housekeeping rules’ embodied in state law”).
2 The United States suggests that the Court’s tradition
of treating state substantive law as binding had ended by 1946.

4


Nor do any of Respondent’s cases  support its
perceived line between “housekeeping” and non -
“housekeeping” laws. Many of them are about 42
U.S.C. § 1983, which preempts state remedies law because its whole purpose is to provide “a different remedy” from state tort law. Monroe v. Pape, 365 U.S.
167, 196 (1961) ( Harlan, J., concurring). Others
simply reflect the modern approach of filling in congressional silence with federal common law —which
often calls upon courts to use state law. Monessen
Southwestern Railway Co mpany v. Morgan (cited at
37, 42), for example, makes clear that “Congress’ silence as to the availability of interest”  on a federal
award “does not, without more” set aside state laws
about interest. 486 U.S. 330, 336 (1988).
Respondent’s remaining cases are similar.
Dooley v. Korean Air Lines (cited at 4 2) is about the
Death on the High Seas Act, which this Court had already held preempts state law and which Dooley says
preempts federal maritime law too. 524 U.S. 116, 120

U.S. Br. 25–26 (citing Holmberg v. Armbrecht, 327 U.S. 392, 395
(1946)). But Holmberg holds only that statutes of limitations
don’t govern claims for equitable relief. See  327 U.S. at 398
(Rutledge, J., concurring). And even if (in hindsight) it might
mark the beginning of this Court’s shift from its original understanding of the role of state law, that shift  was only about the
reasons this Court borrowed state law—whether it was mandatory or discretionary —not about whether it did so. There is no
question that Congress in 1947 would have known federal courts
“resort[ed]” to state law “to give meaning and content to federal
statutes” in various contexts. Davies Warehouse, 321 U.S. at 155;
see also Burks v. Lasker, 441 U.S. 471,  477 (1979) ( noting that
federal law would displace state law only “ where the facts required”); cf. U.S. Br. 25 (citing Burks).

5


(1998). And F.D. Rich Co. v. Industrial Lumber Company (cited at 41) refused to incorporate state law because it found the statute there required a uniform
rule for reasons inapplicable here. See 417 U.S. 116,
127 (1974) (“[O]ften, as here, the parties to Miller Act
litigation have little or no contact . . . with the State
in which the federal project is located.”).
These cases are consistent with the default assumption that state law applies wherever Congress
has not displaced it . To be sure, federal causes of action for damages might not incorporate state-law
measures of damages. But that is because  their context often reveal s Congress’s intent not to use state
law. That’s true of both § 1983 and the Federal Employers’ Liability Act at issue in Chesapeake & Ohio
Railway v. Kelly, 241 U.S. 485 (1916) (cited at 42); cf.
N.Y. Cent. R.R. Co. v. Winfield, 244 U.S. 147, 150
(1917) (holding that the Act “supplant[s]” state remedies). When Congress chooses to provide a remedy for
violations of a particular right, state laws that try to
reduce (or expand) that remedy may well be in conflict.
But § 717f(h) doesn’t bestow any federal rights
on property owners. Instead, the statute grants pipeline companies a federal right to condemn  property.
That means the statute would displace any background state rules that would forbid the companies
from exercising that federal right. But (as explained
below) this Court has always understood the power to
take property as different from —and independent
of—the Fifth Amendment’s  just-compensation requirements. Respondent must therefore point to
something about the statute that displaces North

6


Dakota’s rules about property valuation. As discussed
below, it cannot.
The United States takes a different tack, asking this Court to hold that “States may not directly
regulate the use of” any “power of the Federal government.” U.S. Br. 15. But that’s not what this Court’s
cases say. States may not “regulate the Government
directly[.]” North Dakota, 495 U.S. at 434. C ontractors acting under the government’s orders sometimes
share this immunity. See Hencely v. Fluor Corp., 608
U.S. 31, 146 S. Ct. 1086, 1095 (2026). But private delegees under the Natural Gas Act are neither contractors nor acting under orders. They are private companies that have t he government’s permission to build
private pipelines. No case holds or even suggests that
the government’s immunity automatically extends to
private entities who exercise power with the government’s mere permission. The government asks this
Court to replace the existing rules with one that
sweeps aside state authority the moment Congress allows a private entity to exercise any federal legal authority—whether through regulation, law enforcement, or (as here) litigation. The Court should decline.
In short, the default rule is that state law controls unless something in federal law sets it aside.
That rule does not change simply because the Constitution imposes a limit on Congress’s power—after all,
the Constitution imposes many limits. See Campbell
v. City of Haverhill, 155 U.S. 610, 615 ( 1895) (noting
that a statute of limitations would be unconstitutional insofar as it failed to afford a “reasonable time
to sue”). Instead, like with statutes of limitations or
innumerable other legal questions, Respondent must

7


point to something in either the nature of eminent domain or in the statute itself that requires setting
aside state law. It can do neither.
B. This statute does not displace state
substantive law as the rule for calculating just compensation.
Respondent insists that § 717f(h) displaces
state just -compensation rules, either because “the
right of eminent domain” is a term of art encompassing Fifth Amendment just -compensation rules or because the statute itself reflects a policy of displacing
state law. Each argument is wrong: This Court has
already explained that “the right of eminent domain”
is a distinct concept from the Fifth Amendment’s justcompensation requirement, and nothing about the
statutory scheme suggests it displaces state just-compensation rules.
1. Nothing about “the right of eminent
domain” automatically displaces state
just-compensation law.
a. Respondent (at 2) insists that “ the right of
eminent domain” was, in 194 7, a “term of art” that
inherently required ignoring state law s governing
compensation for land . But it cites no case saying
that. Indeed, to the extent that the phrase  “the right
of eminent domain” had a single fixed meaning at the
time, it simply meant the “power to take private property for public uses.” United States v. Jones, 109 U.S.
513, 518 (1883).  But that’s all. In Jones, this Court
rejected the “ assumption that the ascertainment of
the amount of compensation to be made is an essential element of the power of appropriation.” Ibid. The
Fifth Amend ment’s just -compensation requirement

8


“is no part of the power itself.” Ibid. Instead, the Takings Clause is a “limitation” upon the government’s
exercise of its “right of eminent domain.” Ibid. It, like
the rest of the Bill of Rights, sets a floor below which
the federal government cannot go. Respondent asks
this Court to  assume it (alone among the  Bill of
Rights) also imposes a ceiling on the rights the citizenry can invoke against private parties . But a limitation on Congress’s power cannot, of its own force,
preempt state-law protections.
None of Respondent’s cases say otherwise. Respondent’s eminent -domain cases (with one exception, addressed below) all involve the United States ,
not a private condemnor. That difference matters because the United States is always free to ignore state
law. That power is not some special characteristic of
eminent domain; it is a characteristic of t he United
States. As explained in the opening brief, t he United
States is immune from state law  both because states
cannot regulate the United States directly and because the United States cannot be forced to pay
money without its consent. Opening Br. 15, 28.
And this Court has expressly identified that
general immunity as the source of the government’s
immunity in eminent-domain cases. In United States
v. Bodcaw Co., for example, this Court explained that
a lower court  that had ordered the United States  to
pay fees in a condemnation “necessarily rested its decision on constitutional grounds [because it] is settled
that litigation costs cannot be assessed against the
United States in the absence of statutory authorization.” 440 U.S. 202, 203 n.3 (1979) (per curiam). The
rule is not that the United States cannot be forced to

9


pay in an eminent domain action  without statutory
authorization. It is that the United States cannot be
forced to pay without statutory (or constitutional) authorization.
Respondent’s repeated invocation of United
States v. Miller is therefore unavailing because Miller
simply repeats the baseline rule. That case holds that
statutory language about “practice ” and “procedure”
does not change a condemnee’s substantive right to
compensation “grounded upon the Constitution.” 317
U.S. 369, 379–80 & n.24 (1943). Fair enough. But the
reason a condemnee’s rights are grounded upon the
Constitution in a federal condemnation is still, as
Bodcaw tells us, the fact that the United States cannot otherwise be made to pay money.  See 440 U.S.
at 203 n.3. That says nothing about the rule governing private condemnations by “privately owned corporations” for which “the Government [does not] have
any ownership interest.” United States v. New Mexico,
455 U.S. 720, 740 (1982); see Opening Br. 21–22.
In short, a ll of Respondent’s eminent -domain
cases can be explained by the basic principle that
state law can neither force the federal government to
pay money nor “regulate [it] directly.” North Dakota,
495 U.S. at 434. That explains the outcome in cases
like Miller, where the United States was the plaintiff
and thus presumptively immune from state laws
about just compensation.
Resisting this conclusion, Respondent (at 40 –
41) seeks refuge in United States v. 93.970 Acres of
Land, which refused to apply Illinois election-of-remedies law because “[c]ondemnation involves essential
governmental functions.” 360 U.S. 328, 332 (1959).

10


And so it does —when the United States condemns
land for the Army’s “aerial defense missile” sites. Id.
at 330. But private pipelines are not even a function
of the federal government, let alone an essential one.
And the cases cited in 93 .970 Acres confirm
that its rule applies only to the sovereign, not to private companies. As Respondent observes (at 41), that
case cites “Kohl, Miller, and others” in favor of applying federal law. But t hose “others” squarely embrace
the difference between the United States and a private plaintiff. In the first of the “others,”  this Court
held that “the federal law merchant” and not state
law applies to litigation about “the rights and duties
of the United States” regarding federal commercial
paper. Clearfield Tr . Co. v. United States, 318 U.S.
363, 367  (1943). But in the second, which was also
about federal commercial paper, this Court held otherwise—precisely because the United States was not
a party. See Bank of Am. Nat. Tr. & Sav. Ass’n v. Parnell, 352 U.S. 29 (1956). Without the United States,
the dispute was “purely between private parties and
d[id] not touch the rights and duties of the United
States.” Id. at 33.  That meant state law  governed.
Ibid. In other words, 93.970 Acres stands for the proposition that state law does not apply when the United
States sues in its own name —and that it does apply
when private parties litigate about their own rights
and duties.
Respondent’s argument to the contrary turns
centuries of common  law on its head. Respondent’s
view seems to be that eminent domain is an important
sovereign power  and therefore its delegation automatically comes with all the trappings of sovereignty.

11


But it cites no case saying this, and American courts
historically say the opposite—that eminent domain is
an important sovereign power, and courts must therefore be skeptical of its delegation to private hands,
reading that delegation narrowly to include only the
powers actually given.  Opening Br. 19–20. Because
this Court has rightly treated the power to ignore
state law (and even the right to compensation itself)
as distinct from “the right of eminent domain,” Respondent’s cases about the United States taking land
for itself offer no help.
b. Respondent does, however, muster one case
involving a private condemnor, Cherokee Nation  v.
Southern Kansas Railway Co. , 135 U.S. 641 (1890) .
And, understandably, Respondent places great
weight on that case, twice arguing (at 20 and 27) that
the case answers the question presented here because
the Court saw no role for state law there.
But the Court didn’t consider state law in Cherokee Nation for a more obvious reason: T here was no
state law to consider. The statute in that case authorized taking property only “through the Indian Territory.” 135 U.S. at 642; see also id. at 642–43 (describing route exclusively within modern -day Oklahoma).
The State of Oklahoma did not exist in 1890. See Presidential Proclamation of Nov. 16, 1907, 35 Stat. 2160.
Cherokee Nation stands, at most, for the proposition
that state law does not control where no state has jurisdiction to pro mulgate laws. It does nothing to answer the question presented.
The dearth of cases supporting Respondent’s
position stands in contrast with  the cases—both immediately after the adoption of § 717f(h) and, earlier,

12


interpreting its predecessor in the Federal Power
Act—that treat state law as the source of land valuation for private delegees like the one here.  Opening
Br. 30 –31, 34 . Respondent’s only answer to these
cases (at 18 n.6 and 25 n.10) is to wave them aside as
short on analysis.  And so they are. But the point of
these cases is not their depth of analysis. The point is
their uniformity. If Respondent were correct —if “the
right of eminent domain” meant ignoring state compensation law—one would expect there to be at least
one contemporaneous case saying so. There isn’t.
This is all  in line with the fact that a private
delegee under the Natural Gas Act is treated differently in all sorts of ways. As explained in the opening
brief, easements taken by private delegees are subject
to many state law s, including state law s governing
disputes about the easements’ scope. Opening Br. 39.
Easements taken by the United States, though, would
be governed by the Quiet Title Act. 28 U.S.C. § 2409a.
Agreements to purchase easements (or settlements of
condemnation actions) by private pipeline companies
are contracts governed by state law. Opening Br. 39–
40. But disputes over otherwise-identical agreements
with the federal government are  governed by the
Tucker Act. 28 U.S.C. § 1491.
That’s because (again) the sovereign is different. The United States routinely authorizes private
lawsuits under its Commerce Clause authority  without conferring immunity from state laws. Authorizing
those lawsuits do es not automatically sweep aside
state rules like statutes of limitations, so long as the
state rules are not inconsistent with the federal objective. The question for Respondent is why the same

13


should not be so here . It has found no answer in this
Court’s cases.
c. The role of sovereign immunity in this
Court’s eminent-domain cases also matters  in interpreting the statute through the lens of Kimbell Foods.
In the lower court’s view (and as repeated by Respondent here), § 717f(h)’s silence on just compensation does not leave a “gap” in the statutory scheme
because the silence is automatically filled by the Fifth
Amendment itself. Pet. App. 6a.  That would be true
as to the United States because any decision that the
United States must pay money in a condemnation action “necessarily rest[s] its decision on constitutional
grounds.” Bodcaw, 440 U.S. at 203 n.3.
But nothing in the opinion below or in Respondent’s brief explains why the Bodcaw rule applies
to private entities. When a statute authorizing a condemnation by the United States is silent as to compensation, that silence is filled by the Fifth Amendment because the Fifth Amendment is the only possible authorization for payment —the United States
cannot be made to pay money “in the absence of statutory authorization.”  Ibid. But there is no similar
clear-statement rule for requirements that private
entities pay money. That means that when a statute
authorizing a condemnation by a private entity is silent as to compensation, that silence is silence—and
silence, of its own force, cannot displace state law. Respondent musters no case saying otherwise.

14


2. Section 717f(h) does not reflect a general federal policy of displacing state
just-compensation law.
For all that it argues that preemption is the
wrong model, Respondent insists that § 717f(h) reflects a general legislative policy of setting aside the
“patchwork” of state eminent-domain laws in favor of
uniform federal just -compensation rules. Br. for
Resp. 1–2, 10, 13, 28, 47– 48. Indeed, it even accepts
that state law should be set aside only where congressional policy requires it : In describing this Court’s
early-twentieth-century policy of allowing state compensation law to govern even (sometimes) in federal
condemnations, Respondent explains that it was consistent with this Court’s tradition of recognizing state
law “[i]n the absence of explicit legislative policy cutting across state interests.” Id. at 17–18 n.5 (quoting
Jackson Cnty. , 308 U.S. at  351–52). The difference,
says Respondent, is that a legislative policy cutting
across state interests “is emphatically not absent
here.” Ibid.
Except it is absent. As this Court has already
explained, the point of § 717f(h) was to “remedy  [a]
defect” in the Natural Gas Act, which was that “state
eminent domain procedures . . . were frequently made
unavailable” to the entities authorized to build natural-gas pipelines. PennEast Pipeline Co. v. New Jersey, 594 U.S. 482, 489 (2021). This Court’s understanding of the law’s purpose is consistent with its
plain text and legislative history: It was meant to
make eminent domain procedures available, not to
change or dictate the compensation rules that would

15


govern under those procedures. See Opening Br. 2,
31–33.
That means § 717f(h) necessarily displaces
state laws that would prevent pipeline companies
from condemning land—laws that would mean they
once again had “only an illusory right to build.”
PennEast, 594 U.S. at 489.3 But giving effect to state
property law in this context could not plausibly
prevent pipeline construction . For one thing, l and
acquisition simply isn’t a major driver of pipeline
costs. Historically, the cost of land acquisition has
been a tiny fraction—about seven percent—of overall
onshore pipeline construction costs, dwarfed by the
cost of labor, material, and even “miscellaneous.”
Zhenhua Rui et al ., Historical pipeline construction
cost analysis, 4 Int’l J. Oil, Gas & Coal Tech. 244, 255
(2011). If states may pass laws that “incidentally raise
the costs to the military ,” North Dakota, 495 U.S. at
441, then surely they may use generally applicable
laws to strengthen property rights, even if doing so
imposes negligible costs on private industry.
As explained in the opening brief, states that
want to interfere with pipeline construction have a
variety of ways to do so under existing federal law .
Opening Br.  39. It makes little sense to worry that
states would, in addition, upend their own longstanding valuation rules (upending their own infrastructure projects in the process) in the hopes of affect ing

3 Returning to the language of preemption, state laws
that forbid certificate holders from taking land would “prevent
or frustrate the accomplishment of a federal objective.” Geier v.
Am. Honda Motor Co., 529 U.S. 861, 873 (2000).

16


the smallest line on a pipeline company’s budget. 4
And they haven’t: Until this case, Petitioners’ proposed rule was the unanimous rule in the lower
courts. It has not posed any conflicts with federal objectives in practice. It does not pose any conflicts with
federal objectives even in theory.  Respondent’s repeated, unsupported insistence that the statute reflects a legislative policy of setting aside state law reflects a correct intuition that such a policy is a necessary precondition to setting aside state law. But insisting that the policy exists does not mean it does. It
does not, and the decision below should therefore be
reversed.
C. Respondent’s remaining arguments
lack merit.
Finally, Respondent offers a handful of other
arguments—asking this Court to interpret § 717f(h)
by looking only to language in unrelated statutes,
asking it to read its decision in PennEast to resolve
questions that case never addressed, and  urging the
Court to answer a question other than the question
presented. Each is wrong.

4 Perhaps for this reason, the States that have filed a n
amicus brief supporting Petitioners’ view are not States with any
demonstrated history of seeking to stymie development. See generally Br. for North Dakota, et al. Instead, they are States (like
North Dakota or Texas) that are replete with pipelines but also
concerned with protecting property rights.

17


1. Respondent’s collection of disparate
statutes sheds no light on the best interpretation of this statute.
As explained in the opening brief, Congress directly borrowed the language of § 717f(h) from the
Federal Power Act, under which lower courts had applied state just-compensation law. And this Court has
held that when “Congress copie[s]” language from one
statute, lower-court decisions about that other statute
are relevant to interpreting the new one. Jerman v.
Carlisle, McNellie, Rini, Kramer & Ulrich, L.P.A., 559
U.S. 573, 588–89 (2010). Even where lower -court decisions “may not have ‘settled’ the meaning ” of the
language, this Court has given weight to those decisions where there is “no reason to suppose that Congress disagreed with those interpretations when it enacted the” new law. Id. at 590. Respondent (at 18 &
n.6) insists the early Federal Power Act  cases were
either undermined by Miller or else are too thinly reasoned to warrant this Court’s attention. But Miller,
again, only addressed condemnations by the sovereign, and the lower -court interpretations of the Federal Power Act  s till present unrebutted evidence of
how Congress would have viewed the language it was
borrowing.
Rather than looking to the Federal Power Act,
Respondent invokes various other statutes, ranging
from the General Bridge Act to the Equal Access to
Justice Act, in an effort to show that congressional silence necessarily means using federal just-compensation law. But, in the absence of express borrowing,
this Court has repeatedly rejected this approach.
“Language in one statute usually sheds little light

18


upon the meaning of different language in another
statute, even when the two are enacted at or about
the same time.” Russello v. United States, 464 U.S. 16,
24–25 (1983); see also Gross v. FBL Fin. Servs., Inc.,
557 U.S. 167, 174–75 (2009) (“When conducting statutory interpretation, we must be careful not to apply
rules applicable under one statute to a different statute without careful and critical examination.”
(cleaned up) ); Lindh v. Murphy, 521 U.S. 320, 330
(1997) (“[N]egative implications raised by disparate
provisions are strongest when the portions of a statute treated differently had already been joined together and were being considered simultaneously
when the language raising the implication was inserted.”).
The other statutes Respondent invokes illustrate why this Court generally rejects this sort of loose
comparative approach. Take the General Bridge Act
of 1946, which authorizes condemnations for bridges
over federal navigable waters and provides that compensation for any land taken should be “ascertained
and paid according to the laws” of the state where the
property sits. 33 U.S.C. § 532. That language reflects
the peculiarities of interstate tensions unique to the
historical regulation of bridges, not a rejection of state
law. Both the General Bridge Act and the Natural Gas
Act reflect the same intuition that state law should
govern compensation. The difference is that (in the
bridge context) it originally made sense for Congress
to specify which state’s law controlled.
History explains why. The “ascertained” language in the General Bridge Act mirrors the language
of the North River Bridge Act  of 1890. 26 Stat. 268.

19


While Congress had authorized bridges before 1890,
it had done so only through “license acts from Congress” because the bridges themselves were constructed under “the general railroad laws of the
States.” H.R. Rep. No. 51-928, at 33 (1890). In 1890,
however, Congress sought to authorize the construction of a bridge over the Hudson River, which required
it to create a new corporation  to govern the project,
lest legal disputes between New York and New Jersey
make it impossible to  raise capital for the project.
Ibid. (expressing concern about “conflict and disagreement between the States, arising out of the operation,
regulation, and control of the legal affairs of the company”). Nothing in the statute’s structure or history
suggests that the “ascertained” language was intended to distinguish between state just -compensation law and federal just-compensation law (which, in
1890, had yet to be articulated) . I nstead, Congress
was conce rned with forestalling disputes between
New York and New Jersey about whose law would
govern the newly created entity.
When Congress later tried to standardize the
language used to authorize bridges over navigable
waters, it looked to the North River Bridge Act as a
precedent and incorporated its  “ascertained” language into several of the forms adopted. See Forms for
Bridge Bills, U.S. Cong ressional Serial Set 8558
(1926); 67 Cong. Rec. 8533 (1926) (statement of Rep.
Denison). And that carried forward into the 1946 General Bridge Act,  seemingly without any substantive
discussion at all. This sort of historically contingent
drafting is why this Court declines to use one statute’s
language to interpret another unrelated statute, no
matter when the laws were enacted.

20


Respondent’s other statutory analogies are
even less help  because they speak to the obligations
of the United States. The Uniform Relocation Assistance Act and the  Equal Access to Justice Act (invoked by Respondent at 23) both speak to the United
States’ obligation to pay fees when it (respectively)
abandons a condemnation or takes unreasonable litigation positions.  42 U.S.C. § 4654(a)(2); 28 U.S.C.
§ 2412. But those are specifically obligations imposed
on “the United States” (§ 4654(a)(2)) or  one of its
“agenc[ies] or . . . official[s]” (§ 2412(a)(1)) that say
nothing about private actors’ rights or obligations. Respondent (at 2 3) cites Transwestern Pipeline Co. v.
17.19 Acres, 627 F.3d 1268  (9th Cir. 2010) , for the
proposition that this fee-shifting provision of the URA
“applies to NGA proceedings.” But that case says the
opposite. It holds that where § 4654(a)(2) says “the
United States” it means “the United States” and does
not apply to private condemnors under the Natural
Gas Act. Id. at 1270. In other words, it holds that private condemnors are different from the United States,
in that as in so many other ways . Respondent’s position here seems to be that it is vested with all of the
sovereign’s powers, but only some of the sovereign’s
responsibilities.
To be sure, a different subsection of the URA
sweeps broadly enough to require all federal condemnors—government actors and delegees alike—to  pay
fees when courts rule that they lack the legal right to
take the underlying land. 42 U.S.C. § 4654(a)(1).5 But

5 And even that much seems inadvertent. The URA as a
whole originally applied only to “the government.” Transwestern

21


that is a procedural requirement (which is why it applies only in “Federal court,” ibid. ) and tells us nothing about the underlying substantive law of just compensation. Indeed, a  property owner who defeats a
condemnation does not receive any just compensation
because nothing gets taken . That Congress has  subsequently imposed a blanket procedural requirement
that the losing condemnor pay fees in those circumstances tells us nothing about how to measure just
compensation in takings that succeed.
2. PennEast sheds no light on the question presented.
As explained in the opening brief, this Court’s
decision in PennEast concerned only whether private
pipeline companies are vested with the power to acquire property. It says nothing about the measure of
just compensation. Opening Br. 44– 46. Respondent
insists otherwise. Br. for Resp. 1, 3 –5, 8, 11, 26 –28,
33–36, 38, 40–41, 43, 47. But Respondent’s argument
rests entirely on the idea that “the right of eminent
domain” carries with it Fifth Amendment just- compensation rules. As explained above, this Court has
already said that the power and the required payment
are two distinct concepts. Supra 7–8.

Pipeline Co., 627 F.3d at 1271 (quoting legislative history from
1970 enactment). The portion of the statute that shifts fees for
disallowed condemnations also  applied only to federal agencies
until 1987, when Congress amended a separate portion of the
URA to include private entities in the definition of “federal
agency,” for what appear to be unrelated reasons. See H.R. Conf.
Rep. 100-27, at 244–45 (1987), as reprinted in 1987 U.S.C.C.A.N.
121, 228–29. That history reflects no consideration of—let alone
a determination to reject—substantive state laws.

22


If more is needed, one need look no further than
the analysis in PennEast itself, which holds that
states surrendered their sovereign immunity from
federally authorized eminent-domain lawsuits in “the
plan of the Convention.” 594 U.S. at 50 1. But, at the
risk of stating the obvious, the Fifth Amendment (ratified in 1791) was not part of the plan of the Convention of 1787. The particular “just compensation” principles incorporated in the later- adopted amendment
therefore play no part in PennEast ’s analysis. That
case stands only for the proposition that § 717f(h) does
what Congress wanted it to do (and what its text commands): ensure that federally authorized natural-gas
pipelines have what Jones called the “power to take
private property[.]” 109 U.S. at 518. The statute’s delegation of the power to take is, as the PennEast Court
said, “categorical,” 594 U.S. at 498, but it is only a delegation of the power to take. It says nothing at all
about the measure of compensation.
3. Respondent’s bid to reformulate the
question presented is unfounded.
As a last -ditch effort, Respondent  (at 43– 45)
asks the Court to hold that even if state just-compensation rules generally control, fee- shifting rules
should be treated differently. But that argument was
not addressed below (or, seemingly, by any other appellate court). As a “court of review, not of first view,”
this Court need not reach Respondent’s alternative
question presented. E.g. , Cutter v. Wilkinson, 544
U.S. 709, 718 n.7 (2005).
In any event, the argument fails. If the Fifth
Amendment’s constitutional floor supplies § 717f(h)’s
measure of just compensation, then the reason

23


attorneys’ fees are unavailable is not because of the
American Rule. It’s because this Court has held that
forcing property owners to bear the costs of condemning their property does not fall beneath that constitutional floor. Bodcaw, 440 U.S. at 203–04 & n.3. And if
state law controls the measure of just compensation,
the availability of attorneys’ fees likewise does not
turn on the American Rule  but on whether state law
says the fair value of land encompasses transaction
costs (just as different jurisdictions may have different customs for who bears the cost of a real -estate
agent’s commission). See Opening Br. 47. Either way,
the answer turns on how to measure just compensation, not on the American Rule.
* * *
For decades, lower courts have applied state -
law compensation rules in private condemnations under the Natural Gas Act. Rather than ask Congress to
change the status quo, Respondent asks this Court to
do it. But there is no need for a change. North Dakota
has adopted a broad law that purports to govern property valuation whenever land is taken through force
of law. Congress has said nothing to displace that law
here. That means North Dakota’s law governs, and
the decision below should be reversed.
CONCLUSION
The judgment of the court of appeals should be
reversed.
